content:
I am working on auto-formalization project where I am auto-formalizing a number of ring constructions and theorems from the literature. I have at least 3 cases now where I believe I have errors in the literature where the statement is false and does not appear to be easily fixed, and where no corrigendum exists and no cited work that I found mentions the error. Some of these are more or less minor, e.g. the author published a corrected version of the construction in a later book (but never mentioned that the original construction is wrong) or the paper is wrong but another author gave a different correct construction (citing it as derived from the original paper and not saying the original was wrong.) Beyond the 3 unreported errors, I also have more of the form "known error, but requires a citation search" or "error in the argument that with work is fixable so that the original statement holds."

The authors of these works have passed away so they can't be contacted.

I could spend some time trying to understand these well enough to write them up, but I fear that this would take a lot of time and may not be helpful coming from an outsider that is not an expert in ring theory. I am not sure what the right way to handle this is. To me, it really seems like there should be a central registry of errors indexed by DOI/ISBN, even just to note that a corrigendum exists or to link to an author's errata page. Controlling for quality in such a database seems important and I give no suggestion as to how one should work.

I wanted to bring it up and see if others had thoughts or run into this issue as well.

FWIW I have also found errors in the literature (years ago, before formalisation and AI were big things) which the experts in question claim they know how to fix (typically with unpublished and usually unrefereed letters which are, or were, in my inbox and sometimes by very prestigious people) and my impression is that the mathematical community does not really care at all about these issues. One of the reasons I moved into formalisation was seeing this phenomenon happening at a top level, but essentially every expert I talked to seemed not to care at all about this and I think I was regarded as picky for pointing these things out ("the paper contains important new ideas and we know how to fix the errors" basically). I don't think any of your ideas about DOI etc are going anywhere in practice, the experts don't care, the literature is self-healing, and the experts know the issues anyway (it would not surprise me if your observations are either dismissed as unimportant or known to the experts -- did you talk to an expert?). I think the way to handle this is to play the long game (I've been playing the long game for ten years now) and note that it will only be in a year or two when huge tracts of the literature are being autoformalised and these issues are showing up more often. By that point there will be a far more compelling case for the humans to actually do something, even if it is just "point your robot at the sketch on how to fix this, which was published by someone else/which was informally circulated when the issue became known". That's how maths actually works (at least in my area) and this has been well known for a long time.

It's enough to make you want to change fields and build an undergraduate degree in lean, right?

There are related thoughts by @Alex Meiburg from earlier: #FLT > Anthropic formalization @ 💬 .

Discovering errors in literature is one of the best things we can learn during formalization (at least this is the impression I got since the classic post of Tao's), and they should be double checked and disclosed. The disclosure should even be a standard section of the documentation of an autoformalization project, so people can immediately be informed on what the autoformalization may deviate from the literatures that ground it, be it a proper or ad hoc repair, or even a major obstacle.

My takeaway of Kevin's message above, is that the errata is less informative for the experts in the field unless it has some (unknown and important) consequences, e.g. invalidating some results (like what S6 did to CDP), or the repair involves non-trivial novel techniques that may help other open problems).

As someone who may not have connections to experts in the field, one may just double check (and try to deduce some consequences) to their best effort, then disclose the errata (or just discrepancies) along with the autoformalization, so eventually an agent or a human expert may use or engage with such information.

I agree with Kevin that the experts don't care. However, consider researchers in less developed countries. They may not have access to the experts or to the tools that can easily discover and repair these errors. For their sake, I think it is good to try to document these errors.

How to document them is a more difficult question. There is currently no errata database. With the caveat that policies may have changed since I last checked, I can say that the arXiv won't accept errata unless the original paper is on the arXiv (which may not be the case in your examples), and MathSciNet will document published errata but won't accept "original" errata for publication (and MathSciNet is paywalled anyway). Some journals will insist that errata be submitted by the original author and go through the usual refereeing process.

Three possibilities you could try are: (1) contact the journals and see if they are willing to publish a corrigendum; (2) failing that, if a couple of sentences are sufficient, see if zbMATH is willing to publish those sentences; (3) pioneer an errata database. The last of these is probably the best solution (assuming the journals themselves drag their feet, which I fully expect), but will probably require institutional support to survive any length of time. That said, perhaps the best way to start is for a few people to launch a grass-roots effort and hope that it catches on.

I don't think it would make sense to create a centralized errata database. My proposal above works in an decentralized manner, whoever found it only need to mention the literature and the errata in their formalization project doc, an agent would find the project if it wants to make use of the literature, then it would benefit from the errata.

Furthermore, instead of in the docs, it could part of the standard of #formalization.yaml , thus any registry that collects formalization projects (e.g. Palomar) would contain such information in a structured manner, no need for a standalone errata database, particularly if the long game is "when huge tracts of the literature are being autoformalised".

There was a post in the FLT formalization thread, documenting non-trivial mathematical errors in the FLT-relevant literature that were discovered in the Anthropic formalization (including one in a paper by Livné (?) that sounded potentially quite severe). I really hope this information gets recorded somewhere other than in an ephemeral Zulip post! To me, this list of errata it is one of the most valuable outcomes for the mathematical community of the FLT formalization.

Utensil Song said:

an agent would find the project if it wants make use of the literature, then it would benefit from the errata.

Again, this assumes that researchers in less developed countries have plentiful access to AI. I'm not prepared to assume that. I have nothing against a decentralized system such as you mention, but I think a centralized repository makes sense as well. This is a good moment in history to start such a database, I think, because if it catches on, then it could quickly amass hundreds if not thousands of entries.

This is a good moment in history to start such a database, I think, because if it catches on, then it could quickly amass hundreds if not thousands of entries.

I'm afraid it would amass thousands of trivial typos, while the errors that actually matter would be hushed up, just as they are now. The experts in any given field all know each other; so they avoid criticising each other's work publicly, to avoid upsetting colleagues. Meanwhile, authors who are aware of mistakes in their own papers have every incentive to delay publicly acknowledging the mistake until they can also publicly announce a fix for it – and this will frequently never occur.

Timothy Chow said:

Again, this assumes that researchers in less developed countries have plentiful access to AI. I'm not prepared to assume that. I have nothing against a decentralized system such as you mention, but I think a centralized repository makes sense as well.

I agree. This is one of the reasons that I also proposed to include errata metadata in #formalization.yaml so they can be collected by formalization registries and accessible to anyone able to perform simple search on the registries.

Formalization is possibly the best place to report these errata list because it is objective, independent, verifiable, and likely with the repair.

David Loeffler said:

I'm afraid it would amass thousands of trivial typos, while the errors that actually matter would be hushed up, just as they are now.

That's a legitimate concern. But I think that one could start with some "easy" cases, such as existing published errata that are currently scattered across the literature. Other "good" examples such as the ones mentioned at the beginning of this thread could also be added. If the database gets off to a good start, that can set the tone for future entries, and hopefully stave off some of the "slop".

An amusing typo in the literature: the statement of the polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture in the Annals is incorrect for a trivial reason, despite the fact that it has been formalized. The formal statement in the PFR formalization corrects the error but the informal statement was never fixed (either in the Annals, which is unsurprising, but also not on ArXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05762, which would be more likely to happen). The reason I know this was that my group dutifully translated the theorem as written in the Annals into Lean as part of the Annals Challenge project, and then our AI adversarial review came up with a counterexample :-)

In fact our forthcoming paper flags 10 such typos in Annals theorems, incriminating, amongst other people, 4 Fields Medallists, but mathematicians are used to this sort of thing and do not attach any importance to it.

I recently heard a prediction of 10bn lines of Lean to autoformalize all of extant mathematics, expected to be completed by the end of 2027. Would it change the incentives if say 5% of papers are put on the "not autoformalized" pile? Will anyone ever reexamine those and try to fix the glitches?
Oh sure! If we have a "naughty list" of papers (and before long I think we will have!) then people are going to start asking questions.

There is a pest from MathOverflow who has been feeding papers into ChatGPT and finding errors, then gets the AI to write it up and posts a Zenodo preprint. I've been sent two emails, one was an issue that was just being a little sloppy, a prior paper described the correct definition, the other was a false lemma that wasn't actually needed, but the consequence of applying it is, I'm sure, still true, and his counterexample to the lemma doesn't break the following propositions. The first isn't worth a journal correction, but I'll put a footnote in the arXiv version. The second I'll get an addendum. But I'm small fry. This guy has stuff on Perelman, Zahl, Atiyah (his flawed RH paper, like that even needed to be done), more famous conjectures' proofs.

While this is to some extent valuable, anyone with a subscription could do this, and it's a service to the community at best, there's zero mathematical expertise needed, except perhaps to write up the erratum document in a way that's not AI slop and pitched at the appropriate level. The more useful bit would be to actually show why the theorems intended are still true, not that some edge case in a lemma was missed due to an implicitly assumed condition that everyone takes for granted, and giving a pedestrian and painfully-explained counterexample exploiting that edge case. If anyone wants a link I can DM to his author page to see the type of stuff I mean.

Possible issues with errata databases that require the original authors to agree with any errata include:

  • Won't work with authors who are no longer active / contactable.
  • Authors wanting to cover up errors until they have fixes.
  • Authors disagreeing with general community consensus that there is in fact a flaw in the paper.

Possible issues with errata databases that don't require approval from the original authors include:

  • Bogus errata from cranks.
  • Bogus errata from people with a personal animosity to the original authors.
  • Bogus errata from people who misunderstood the paper (including e.g. missing an explanation of common conventions 100 pages earlier that's needed to get the correct mathematical meaning of a lemma).
  • Errata where it's technically true that some particular detail isn't explained in the paper, but that's consistent with usual practice in the field for the level of detail to give and what readers are expected to fill in for themselves, not enough to be considered an actual gap in the paper in normal usage.
  • Journals interpreting an erratum (bogus or not) as being more significant than it actually is, and issuing a retraction (even if the paper is actually wrong, withdrawing it from availability is a bad idea, it may well still have useful things in it) or (invalid) correction of their own accord (cf. how Amazon has reportedly been known to remove self-published books if they receive too many (bogus) reports of typos in them).

I think having a central way to track known corrections to papers (with the expectation that a large proportion of papers would in fact have at least one minor correction not affecting their main substance - and a strong rule that if the paper isn't yet formally published, having the authors put up a revised arXiv version with the fix makes a lot more sense than adding something to an errata database) would still be useful despite those issues - but it can't be assumed that all errata (or objections to errata) are correct, useful, in good faith or have agreement on their validity, and so it's not enough just to accumulate errata sent in, any such database would need need to have a way to discuss their merits, track disputes over errata and deal with incompetent and bad-faith contributors (both human and AI), which would probably be much the harder part of the problem compared to simply having a mapping from papers to errata in those papers.

"Can't autoformalize" would also include things that aren't even clearly errata in that specific paper. Is it an erratum for a paper to depend on some other preprint that was announced 20 years ago and never released? If paper X has a theorem whose proof is fatally flawed (but that is still thought likely to be true), is that just an erratum in paper X, or is it also an erratum in every other paper that has a result using that theorem, directly or indirectly (some of which might be much more readily fixable than others not to use that theorem)? Both of those mean no complete proof in the literature, but "depends on something missing / broken" feels different from "mistake directly in this paper" (after all, the later paper correctly proves something, it's just that what's proved is a conditional result where the condition is something unpublished or with no known proof).

Note that some authors are intentionally incorrect (or, at least, imprecise) for pedagogical reasons. It is quite common to say "We treat definition X as basically being the same as Y" or "This theorem is evidently true due to X, but a rigorous proof requires Y". Good authors leverage preexisting intuition to make their subject more accessible to a wider audience, even if this obscures technical details which would be caught by formalization.

My opinion is that informal math should stay informal. We should be okay with papers skipping over details, making harmless mistakes, using arguments that aren't technically sound as long as they remain morally true. If the goal is to find out what is literally true, we ought to abandon papers altogether--focus on formalized mathematics, and build tools to informalize our massive Lean libraries so that humans can understand them. But do not expect literature to fill this role.

Adam Topaz said:

Utensil Song could you please open an issue on the #formalization.yaml repo?

Opened as mathlib-initiative/formalization.yaml#27.

I proposed small schema changes and provided worked examples for errata in #FLT > Anthropic formalization @ 💬 (requested by @Alex Meiburg , documented by @Ralph Furman ) .

The short worked example looks like this (the full errata example is at the bottom of the issue):

# Two changes: `relationship: repair` in sources, and a new `errata` key.

sources:
  - title: "On Ihara's modular group"
    authors: ["Jens Mennicke"]
    id: "doi:10.1007/BF01425756"
    type: "article"
    location: "Invent. Math. 4 (1967), 202-228"
    relationship: adapts

  - title: "The Schur multiplicator of SL(2, Z/mZ) and the congruence subgroup property"
    authors: ["F. Rudolf Beyl"]
    id: "doi:10.1007/BF01163607"
    type: "article"
    location: "Math. Z. 191 (1986), 23-42"
    relationship: repair

errata:
  - source: "doi:10.1007/BF01425756"
    location: "Schur multiplier of SL(2, Z/m)"
    statement: "The Schur multiplier of SL(2, Z/m) vanishes for all m."
    lean: ""
    note: "It fails whenever 4 divides m, where it is Z/2."
    repair:
      source: "doi:10.1007/BF01163607"
      note: >-
        Ihara's lemma is proved from Beyl's computation of the multiplier
        (Z/2 when 4 | m, trivial otherwise) and his repair of the argument,
        not from Mennicke's vanishing claim.
You could try an endorsement system like arXiv to help keep cranks out of a public errata database

Utensil Song said:

I proposed small schema changes and provided worked examples for errata in #FLT > Anthropic formalization @ 💬 (requested by Alex Meiburg , documented by Ralph Furman ) .

I just opened https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/formalization.yaml/pull/28/, I'd love a review on this
Interesting, in the PR, Claude pointed out that https://github.com/rkirov/enumerative-chromatic-choosability/blob/main/formalization.yaml has used an alternative errata format which may be inspiring.

@Utensil Song (I'll comment this on the issue as well), I think for the relationships it's not clear to me how to bucket all types of errata into "repairs" or "adapts". Do you have an example of how one would record that for example, a paper proves an iff and a later paper notes that the backwards half of the proof is wrong (and whether the backwards statement is true is still an open question)? I wouldn't call this a repair or an adaptation, but maybe I am thinking of a repair as fixing the proof so that the statement holds rather than crossing out part of it that doesn't.
In some cases, a paper claims X but I prove not X (and it is not a matter of adding trivial hypotheses/fixing typos to get back to X.) How should that be recorded?

"Adapts" is one of the existing types for a source. The short example simply inherited it, for the purpose of demonstration you can think of it as an ordinary source.

In your first example (proving the other half of an iff) is clearly not a repair, because there was nothing wrong, in the sense that may have consequences on correctness of things that build on it.

In your second example (disproving another paper's claim), if the disproof comes with a Lean formalization repo, it certainly should log an entry of errata in formalization.yaml . Of course, later it may turn out that the Lean formalization was wrong, so the errata is wrong.

An update on my comments above, because I think it's illustrative, and I'm working through the fix. The paper with the actual erroneous lemma (which I believe was found by AI), actually has more obvious flaw: at one point I wrote down what amounts to an isomorphism of one geometric object with a more nuts-and-bolts constructed geometric object (both sides are infinite-dimensional manifolds) and treated the RHS as the working definition of the (very opaque) LHS. The only problem is... the RHS is not the same thing as the LHS, and it's obvious after a moment's thought that part of the iterated pullback construction is missing, and moreover is nontrivial to establish that the construction works/is justified; it's not just a typo, in other words.

So the (suspected) AI found the lemma was wrong, and gave a counterexample to it, but it didn't notice that the definition of the family of objects being discussed wasn't correct. A bit like autoformalising the wrong definitions but then making watertight theorems about them, in reverse.

And neither did the referee, for that matter! To be fair, it was a 47-page paper with a real spread of topics...

I think my agent just made that up. I asked it to conform to the schema and it switched to fidelity > divergences - https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/formalization.yaml/blob/main/schema/v0.4.schema.json#L307C6-L307C14 which doesn't seem quite the same but at least it conforms.

@Jack McCarthy Is mathlib-initiative/formalization.yaml#28 ok to merge or do we need to ping some reviewers? Maybe we can merge it and evolve during realworld adoptions, as this is an optional in the spec.

For earlier discussions: relationship discussion is resolved; also it now no longer conflicts with Rado Kirov's errata style. It is consistent with the style of the rest of the spec, and agents seem to be able to handle these well enough in light of Rado Kirov's case.
